Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette:
Tran was sixteen when the soldiers came. His village lay along a contested supply route, and the morning the mortar fire stopped, three men in uniforms he did not recognise dragged him from his family’s shed. They tied his wrists behind his back with nylon cord and forced him to kneel in the mud. The cord bit into his skin every time he shifted. One of the soldiers screamed at him in a language he half-understood—something about hidden weapons—while another kicked over a drum of cooking oil that caught fire. The smell of burning fat and kerosene filled his nostrils, thick and greasy, and stayed long after the soldiers left him untied and bleeding. He never knew why they let him go. He never told anyone the full story.

Seventy years later, Tran worked the night shift at a regional warehouse, stacking boxes of canned goods onto pallets. The building was cavernous and poorly ventilated, and the air always carried the faint, rancid scent of spilled cooking oil from a damaged shipment two years ago. Tran tried to avoid that aisle, but the forklift drivers rotated routes, and sometimes the smell would hit him without warning. When it did, the memory of the burning drum returned whole and unfiltered—the cord around his wrists, the soldier’s spittle on his cheek, the heat against his face. The memory was so vivid, so detailed, that he would stop whatever he was doing, frozen, his chest tight and his hands trembling. He had to set down the box and walk to the breakroom, breathing through his mouth, until the images faded.

The memory itself made him more watchful. After an episode, he could not stand being in a narrow aisle between two tall racks—the walls seemed to close in, and he felt a phantom pressure around his wrists. He began to avoid those aisles entirely, clocking in early to study the floor plan and memorise which bays were wide-open. But the avoidance only sharpened his sensitivity. A coworker once confronted him about missing a pallet label, raising his voice only slightly, and Tran’s mind jumped instantly back to the soldier screaming. The confrontation—the raised tone, the anger—became a new trigger, almost as potent as the smell. He started eating lunch alone in the parked delivery truck, where no one could corner him. 

The causal loop tightened over months. A trigger—a smell, a tense conversation, a moment of being trapped between shelves—would throw him into the memory. And the memory, raw and overwhelming, left him so hypervigilant that he scanned every aisle for the next threat, his shoulders braced for a hand on his arm. He once felt a forklift operator tap his shoulder to ask him to move, and he flinched so hard he dropped a crate of glass jars. The sound of shattering glass sent his heart hammering, and he had to leave the floor for the rest of his shift.

What finally brought Tran to the clinic was not the fear itself, but the cost. His supervisor had written him up for three “unexplained absences” from his station—spells when he had to retreat to the truck. Tran knew he could not afford to lose this job, the only thing that gave his solitary days structure. He sat in the intake chair with his hands clasped, his voice low, and described the smell of cooking oil, the feeling of a cord that was no longer there, and the certainty that his mind was winding a trap he could not escape.
